newsitem.title: USA: Attacks by hair-munching dolls alarm safety experts.
newsitem.headline: Attacks by hair-munching dolls alarm safety experts.

text.p: Federal safety officials Monday were investigating a rash of incidents where battery operated Cabbage Patch dolls reportedly chewed up little girls' hair.
Spokesman Ken Giles said the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission would issue a statement Monday about the dolls, which safety experts said posed a danger to children.
Giles, however, did not expect the agency to order a recall of the Mattel Inc. doll.
"It ought to be recalled," product liability attorney Edward Swartz said. "Kids are going to experiment with that toy, and entanglement injuries are being reported."
At least seven girls around the country have caught their hair inside Mattel Inc.'s "Cabbage Patch Snack Time Kid", thousands of which were sold over Christmas.

Emily Newton of Tavares, Fla., was the latest victim of the hair-eating dolls. Her doll was supposed to eat plastic celery sticks but instead it gnawed on an 8-inch strand of Emily's waist-length auburn hair Friday night, Emily's mother, Peggy Newton, said Monday.
The four-year-old's parents were able to remove the hair from the doll's mouth without injuring Emily or cutting her hair.
Other incidents have resulted in bald spots, shorn hair, scalp welts, and some tears but no lawsuits as yet. Swartz said one girl caught her finger in the doll's masticating mouth.
Engineers from Mattel were meeting with the commission, a spokewoman for the El Segundo, California-based toy manufacturer said.
"All of our products undergo rigorous testing," Mattel spokeswoman Lisa McKendall said, adding that inserting only hair into the mouth should not have triggered the chewing mechanism.

Lifting off the doll's plastic backpack will stop the chewing action, McKendall said, while removing the batteries requires unscrewing several screws. Some frantic parents have taken the doll apart, ripping off its head.

The doll, a battery-powered version of one that was a huge hit with kids during Christmas in 1984, is designed to "eat" plastic french fries and other fake food and deposit it in the doll's backpack. Mattel has licensed the rights to the Cabbage Patch doll for the past three years.
Swartz blamed the toy industry for unneccesarily mechanizing a once-popular doll that required children to use their imaginations.

Last week, a doll belonging to Sarah Stevens, 7, of Griffith, Indiana, near Chicago chewed her hair up to the scalp and was taken apart screw by screw. The girl said she only hugged the dull to her head when it began gobbling up her long locks.
"This is clearly an intended consequence of a feeding doll, and it is giving the media a feeding frenzy," said Heather Paul, director the National Safe Kids Campaign, a non-profit interest group.
She was glad parents were becoming aware of the potential risk, and suggested they exercise constant supervision over their children while playing with the doll.
